newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN delays Cambodia entry but will admit Burma.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN delays Cambodia entry but will admit Burma.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Thursday postponed Cambodia's membership, saying it still recognised Prince Norodom Ranariddh as co-premier despite his ouster by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
"ASEAN will continue to regard Ranariddh as co-premier of Cambodia," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters after chairing an emergency meeting on the Cambodian crisis.
However, in a joint declaration the ASEAN foreign ministers said the grouping would still admit Burma and Laos later this month as scheduled.

ASEAN's statement reiterated the grouping's policy of not interfering in a neighbouring country's internal affairs, but said the use of force in the feud between Hun Sen and Ranariddh made it necessary to delay Cambodia's entry indefinitely.
At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded last weekend in clashes between forces loyal to Hun Sen and those with Ranariddh.
Abdullah said it was not easy for ASEAN to make the decision.

"We had a long discussion, various views were expressed," he said after the six- hour meeting. "Our policy of non-interference remains...but there's a dramatic change in the political situation in Cambodia and that has been brought about by the use of military force."
In Cambodia, a government spokesman said ASEAN's decision was regrettable and hoped it would not encourage further conflict in his country.
"We regret it very much, but we hope ASEAN won't encourage the fighting in Cambodia," Secretary of State for Information Khieu Kanharith told Reuters.
In Phnom Penh, Hun Sen told reporters before the decision to delay membership was announced that Cambodia's troubles were "our internal business".
"ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."

Hun Sen denied he had staged a coup and said Ranariddh, in Paris when the fighting began, could return to Phnom Penh "to face court". He did not say what sort of legal proceedings Ranariddh might face if he returned.

The ASEAN meeting decided that Philippines Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas and Thai Foreign Minister Rachuab Chaiyasarn should fly to Beijing soon to meet Cambodia's head of state, King Norodom Sihanouk, to discuss how to end the crisis.
Sihanouk is in China undergoing medical treatment.
"We'll get in touch with his majesty King Sihanouk and the indication is the earlier the better. After that, we'll get in touch with the co-premiers," Siazon told reporters.

Alatas said delaying Cambodia's admission was "a practical decision". "We did not pass judgement on who is right, who is wrong, who is legitimate or who is illegitimate or whether there was a coup d'etat," he told reporters after the meeting.
ASEAN had been planning to admit Cambodia along with Burma and Laos at its annual meeting later this month.

The decision to admit Burma was heavily criticised by Western governments and human rights groups that want to isolate Rangoon over its human rights record and its crackdown on a democracy movement led by Aung San Suu Kyi.
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
